Senses.PreferredTarget: The more I look up, the higher it rises; the more I bore into it, the harder it becomes
AlternateTargets: Look up, and it rises higher; drill into it, and it grows firmer
SearchAliases: higher the more one looks harder the more one drills
Senses.Note: The saying describes a subject that increases in height when one looks up to it and in difficulty when one tries to bore into it. Chan speakers apply the familiar pair to a teaching that cannot be exhausted by a simple measure, and sometimes turn it back on a student as a direct question.

Senses.Explanation: The more I look up, the higher it rises; the more I bore into it, the harder it becomes pictures a matter that cannot be exhausted by a simple approach. Yuansou opens a hall speech with the pair and asks what it points to. Linquan uses it while commenting on an old answer whose full point he says must be seen directly. Linye joins it to an old description of what is just before one but cannot be grasped. Baichi makes the pair his answer to a question at a public celebration. Yezhu places it in his own hall verse with images of a mirror and an unbroken line. Shaweng says it from the teaching seat, then asks the assembly to identify what it names.

Senses.Explanation: “Yangshan tipped out a whole basketful” answers the East Temple’s request for one sea-calming pearl by multiplying the requested treasure. Foyan Qingyuan reports his own realization of this answer after Yuanwu Keqin pressed the contradiction in Yangshan’s pearl case. Zhongfeng Mingben sets the basketful beside a shout and a whole canon and asks whether such words are rubble or treasure. Tian’an Sheng raises the pearl case, distinguishes pearl from rubble, and calls Yangshan’s basketful an enhancement of the Chan seat. Wuyi Yuanlai places the answer in verse and asks for the mind that is originally buddha.

Senses.Explanation: “Yangshan asks Zhongyi” labels the encounter in which Yangshan Huiji asks Zhongyi Hong’en about buddha-nature. Zhongyi compares a room with six windows and a monkey inside answering calls from outside. Yangshan then asks how the outside monkey can meet it when the inner monkey sleeps; Zhongyi comes down, grasps Yangshan, and says they have met. Hongzhi Zhengjue verses the sleeping monkey and the reopening of spring. Wansong Xingxiu emphasizes Yangshan’s counter-question after the easy explanation. Dahui Zonggao and Yulin Tongxiu each raise the case in live exchanges and add their own tests. Poshan Haiming also raises the case, criticizes Zhongyi for naming buddha-nature and monkey, and adds a verse.
Senses.Note: Treat this as a case label. The six-window monkey is Zhongyi’s analogy; Yangshan’s sleeping-monkey question turns the encounter.

Hongzhi puts the pair in a verse about a command being issued, and later masters adapt it in verses, sermons, and direct answers. Senses.Explanation: Within the realm the emperor's edict governs; beyond the frontier the general's command does. Donglin Yan, Cuiyan Kezhen, Yuan'an Liao's questioner, and Chulin Shangrui use that division in cases about speaking and silence, commands taking effect, and Nanquan's uncompromising acts. Donglin Yan gives the pair after raising Fengxue's answer about passing through speech and silence. Cuiyan Kezhen uses it while distinguishing Xuefeng's handling from his own. An unnamed questioner presents it to Yuan'an Liao as the frame for asking when a tally arrives and an order takes effect. Chulin Shangrui verses it after Nanquan's actions.
